news_drafts.headline: Grampian Valuation Joint Board forecasts £705,000 underspend on £5.653m 2026/27 budget
news_drafts.lead:
Grampian Valuation Joint Board is forecasting that it will end 2026/27 with £705,000 less spent than its approved day-to-day budget (revenue budget) of £5.653m. Its budget monitoring statement (the in-year check of spending against budget) for 1 April to 30 September 2026 shows net expenditure of £2.25m to 30 September and a year-to-date surplus of £577,000. The paper says that position reflects vacancies and the timing of expenditure, and that the estimated outturn (the actual figures for the year, once it has ended) gives a more representative year-end view.

The board's financial planning paper puts the estimated 2026/27 outturn at £4.948m and attributes the favourable position largely to staffing vacancies and the timing of expenditure. It notes that a number of costs and commitments remain uncertain and will be reviewed during budget setting. The 2026/27 requisitions, the sums the board asks its constituent councils to pay, were set at £5.653m on 30 January 2026. The monitoring paper says the final position depends on expenditure in the remaining months.

Any 2026/27 surplus remaining after the external audit (an independent check on the accounts) and approval of the annual accounts will be returned to the constituent authorities in proportion to their requisitions, according to both papers. The board did the same last year. Its external audit annual report gives 2025/26 net expenditure of £5.038m, an underspend of £0.536m against budget. The surplus was £0.379m, of which £0.313m was returned to constituent authorities. The paper says the full approved use of reserves was not required.

news_drafts.headline: Moray bus service passenger journeys rise 86% as council maintains £686,435 annual subsidy into revised Phase 3
news_drafts.lead: Moray Council's bus service has delivered 86 per cent growth in passenger journeys since the project began, rising from 45,881 in 2022/23 to 85,309 in 2025/26. Farebox income — the money paid by passengers — has grown at 22.6 per cent annually in the first four months of the current financial year. The council reported that revenue performance is tracking at approximately 98 per cent of the original model assumptions and is forecast to exceed £360,000 per annum. The council is maintaining its annual subsidy of £686,435 despite revising Phase 3 strategy from network expansion to analytical development, focusing on data tools, performance monitoring and service optimization. The paper notes the Scottish Government's £2 fare cap, introduced in March 2026, has contributed to passenger growth and farebox income by improving affordability while the government reimburses operators. The revised Phase 3 budget is grounded in actual operating costs and observed demand from Phases 1 and 2, rather than the assumptions in the original business case.
news_drafts.paper_title: Bus Revolution Strategic Approach and Revenue Budget Phase 3

news_drafts.headline: Moray Council transport audit finds insurance gap affecting 2,700 pupils
news_drafts.lead: Moray Council's auditors have identified significant control gaps in home to school transport, which serves about 2,700 pupils. An internal audit review found that while insurance is verified when contracts start, no annual checks confirm cover remains valid during the contract period. The same review identified other management failures: one contract variation (a formal change to existing contract terms) worth approximately £86,450 annually was not subject to the required competitive tendering process, contract extensions were not formally documented before 2024–25 and only approximately 40 per cent were documented in 2025–26, and transport providers were underpaid by approximately £10,000 due to a calculation error. The council has accepted audit recommendations to implement annual insurance verification by 31 March 2027, complete all contract documentation by 31 July 2026, and clarify the correct payment amount.
news_drafts.paper_title: Internal Audit Review - Home to School Transport

findings.headline: The pension asset exceeded the pension liability by £15.522 million, and the IFRIC 14 assessment reduced the recognised asset to nil
findings.detail: The paper says the actuary's IFRIC 14 assessment capped the asset at nil for reporting purposes only, with the actuary's position still a net asset at 31 March 2026. The updated actuary report led to a £97,000 disclosure change with no net impact on the accounts.
findings.matters: A finance director comparing pension positions across councils will want to see how a net surplus is treated under IFRIC 14 when the employer cannot access it.
findings.figures: Pension asset exceeds pension liability by £15.522 million; disclosure change of £97,000
findings.quote: This was the case for Grampian VJB, where the pension asset exceeded the pension liability by £15.522 million.

findings.headline: The 2024/25 asset revaluation recommendation has been closed
findings.detail: The board engaged the new valuer early, and the valuer met the requirements for the 2025/26 revaluation exercise. The valuer responded to audit queries within the agreed timescales.
findings.matters: Closing an audit recommendation on valuations, after the valuer changed, is a useful example for councils that share a valuation team with a joint board.

findings.headline: Grant Thornton intends to issue an unmodified opinion on 30 October 2026, subject to outstanding PPE sample evidence
findings.detail: The paper says the audit is substantially complete and that no matters have been identified that would require modification of the opinion. The outstanding item is sample evidence for existence testing of property, plant and equipment, requested in March 2026.
findings.matters: Whether an opinion is unmodified is a basic signal of accounts quality, and an open evidence request on PPE is a point other joint boards also face.
findings.figures: Opinion date 30 October 2026; outstanding PPE sample evidence requested in March 2026
findings.quote: We intend to issue an unmodified opinion on the financial statements on 30 October 2026, subject to the satisfactory completion of the following items:

findings.headline: The 2025/26 audit was delivered later than the Audit Scotland target of the end of September
findings.detail: The paper says the audit was scheduled for September to October 2026 because council staff were focusing on the main council audit first. The final report is to go to the board on 30 October 2026.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council will want to know the timing pressure that a joint board's smaller finance team faced in meeting the statutory deadline.
findings.figures: Audit Scotland target: end of September 2026; audit timetable September to October 2026; final report 30 October 2026
findings.quote: the audit would be delivered in a later cycle than the Audit Scotland target timelines (by the end of September) due to council staff focusing on the main council audit first.

findings.headline: Grampian VJB forecasts a £0.705 million underspend against its 2026/27 budget
findings.detail: The October 2026 monitoring position shows a £0.577 million underspend against the year-to-date budget at the end of September. The paper says the forecast underspend is mainly due to staff vacancies.
findings.matters: A forecast underspend that depends on vacancies, rather than on savings in delivery, shows how a board's in-year position can move with recruitment.
findings.figures: Forecast underspend £0.705 million for 2026/27; year-to-date underspend £0.577 million at end of September 2026; employee cost underspend £0.328 million year to date
findings.quote: The latest forecast projects an underspend of £0.705 million against the approved budget at year-end.
